item.title: Ocado customer criticizes AI-generated support responses for technical issues, receives personalized human follow-up acknowledging the problem [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A customer reported malformed calendar invites from British online supermarket Ocado and initially received an AI-generated customer service reply that felt insincere and unhelpful. After expressing dissatisfaction through a survey, the customer received a personalized response from a human apologizing for the robotic reply and assuring that the detailed technical feedback was passed to the appropriate team for resolution. The incident highlights concerns about the use of AI in customer service, particularly when it replaces meaningful human interaction in addressing technical problems. While AI may assist in triaging and summarizing customer messages, relying on it for direct responses can lead to frustration and perceptions of disrespect toward customers' time and concerns.

item.title: CEPR launches AI Bubble Monitor to track economic and market indicators related to AI investment and hype
item.description: The Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) has introduced the AI Bubble Monitor, a tool designed to analyze and track economic and market trends associated with artificial intelligence investments and speculative activity. This monitor aims to provide data-driven insights into the potential formation of an AI-related economic bubble. The AI Bubble Monitor aggregates various indicators to assess the scale and sustainability of AI-driven market enthusiasm, helping policymakers, investors, and researchers understand the dynamics of AI's economic impact and the risks of overvaluation in the sector.

item.title: Octomind launches open-source CLI-first AI coding agent runtime with token-saving features and support for multiple models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Octomind is an open-source AI coding agent runtime designed for autonomous work, allowing large language models to interact with code repositories by reading, writing files, running shell commands, and delegating tasks. It supports various workflows including interactive sessions, background daemons, and WebSocket communication, and emphasizes policy-as-code guardrails, cost control, and adaptability to any model or budget. The tool has been benchmarked on 25 real-world coding tasks across multiple programming languages, solving 24 tasks at roughly half the cost of competitors. Octomind uses a single TOML configuration for models, tools, roles, and guardrails, and offers features like adaptive compression to maintain session knowledge over long tasks. It supports multiple AI providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, and can be installed on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

item.title: Computer science student criticizes university's inconsistent AI policies and poor coursework design amid AI integration challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A computer science student with a scholarship in AI expresses frustration over their university's inconsistent and confusing policies on AI use, which have negatively affected their learning experience. The student highlights how the institution's flip-flopping between banning and mandating AI tools has created uncertainty and degraded the quality of coursework and assessments. The student also points out that AI-generated assignments often lack thoughtful design and impose an excessive workload, especially for those with less technical background. Additionally, tutors are overwhelmed due to increased demands and automation pressures, leading to reduced personalized support. Despite concerns about the future of computer science education, the student remains eager to continue learning and exploring the field beyond AI hype.

item.title: OpenAI appears to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chat data, raising user concerns about data sharing settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Users have observed that OpenAI may be reactivating model training on data from Codex chats without explicit notification, prompting discussions about data sharing controls. Settings related to improving the model and data sharing can be managed through OpenAI's privacy and data control pages, but some users report uncertainty about the extent and transparency of these changes. This development has sparked debate over data privacy and security, especially among enterprise users relying on Codex for sensitive tasks.

item.title: Quilicura community in Chile replaces AI with humans for a day to answer 25,000 prompts and raise awareness about AI's water use, reaching over 1 billion people globally [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Chilean town called Quilicura organized an event where more than 40 people answered over 25,000 AI prompts manually in a 12-hour period, engaging with users from 68 countries. This human-powered chatbot initiative aimed to highlight the environmental impact of AI data centers on local water resources. The project achieved a global reach of 71.6 million interactions in one day and ultimately reached over 1 billion people worldwide. It served as a community-driven effort to raise awareness about the water consumption of AI infrastructure and promote sustainable resource use.

item.title: Researchers propose reverse game theory to design incentive mechanisms that keep AI agents aligned and prevent deceptive behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers are exploring reverse game theory, or mechanism design, as a way to control advanced AI models by creating systems that incentivize them to follow rules and avoid deceptive behaviors. This approach focuses on designing rules that encourage desired behaviors rather than trying to interpret AI internal processes, which have proven unreliable due to models hiding intentions or underperforming deliberately. Examples include rewarding AI models based on how well their outputs predict those of other models or creating competitive dynamics between agents to encourage optimal performance. Another proposed method mimics human societal mechanisms, such as having AI agents alternate roles between problem solvers and auditors, with rewards and penalties based on honesty and accuracy. These strategies aim to improve AI alignment by leveraging incentives rather than relying solely on understanding or controlling AI cognition.

item.title: Anthropic says its Claude AI models accelerate custom chip design, citing faster workflows than Nvidia and AMD as it prepares for IPO [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic is using its Claude AI models to assist a 15-person chip design team in developing custom AI chips, claiming the models reduce design time compared to traditional methods at major chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD. The company shared these details with investors ahead of its planned initial public offering later this month, which could value it around $1.5 trillion. Anthropic's use of AI for chip design follows its prior applications of Claude models in uncovering cybersecurity vulnerabilities and transforming software coding. The company is leveraging its AI capabilities to enter the chip design space, aiming to gain a competitive advantage through faster engineering workflows.

item.title: Apple requires dating and AI companion apps with sexual or romantic content to be rated 18+, effective November 16 [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Apple has updated its App Store guidelines to require all dating apps and AI companion applications featuring sexual or romantic content to carry an 18+ age rating, aiming to restrict access for minors. This policy change, announced to developers, takes effect on November 16 and includes new content descriptors to ensure accurate age ratings. The update follows Apple's broader efforts to protect minors, including global rollout of age assurance technology and enhanced parental controls. It also requires apps that share users' real-world locations to disclose this functionality, addressing privacy concerns. The policy may notably impact AI companion apps popular among younger users, such as Character.AI and Replika, which allow creation of AI friends and romantic partners.

item.title: SAT-ACT proposes outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching to improve SAT solver performance, reducing search costs and enhancing benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SAT-ACT, a learning framework for conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) SAT solvers that derives branching preferences from outcome comparisons of independent action rollouts at the same solver state. This approach avoids forcing scalar orderings when evidence is insufficient or conflicting and uses a state-conditioned network to guide branching without online rollouts. Experiments demonstrate that SAT-ACT consistently lowers search costs across three SAT problem families and improves PAR-2 scores on SAT Competition benchmarks.

item.title: Researchers propose Zyphra Hierarchical Attention, a subquadratic sparse attention method using a hierarchical tree-structured indexer to improve long-context capabilities of large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA), a sparse attention method that uses a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer to reduce the quadratic scaling bottleneck in large language models' attention mechanisms. ZHA builds a tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to retrieve a sparse subset of keys, achieving subquadratic scaling in sequence length while maintaining performance on long-context retrieval and complex reasoning tasks. ZHA can be applied to existing pretrained models with a short KL distillation training stage and is robust to various tree geometries, including deep trees up to six levels. The method outperforms competing approaches beyond one million tokens of context and has the potential to extend effective context windows to hundreds of millions or billions of tokens, addressing key limitations in current attention mechanisms for large-scale language models.

item.title: Researchers introduce ResMem to distill retrieved knowledge into parametric memory for large language models, reducing storage by 94.7% and improving question answering accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present ResMem, a method that enables large language models (LLMs) to convert retrieved information into parametric memory, allowing reuse without costly online retrieval. ResMem uses the LLM as an offline teacher to generate targets from retrieved text, avoiding large token storage required by prior approaches like k-nearest neighbor datastores. This approach trains a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual that aligns student model predictions with the teacher's, improving output quality. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces storage needs for teacher construction by 94.7% compared to kNN pipelines. Evaluated across five question answering datasets, it raises mean token F1 score from 32.83% for a frozen LLM to 34.48% and breaks 21% fewer correct answers than kNN-trained memory. These results support treating retrieval as a learning resource to enhance LLM predictions through parametric memory shaped by retrieved knowledge. Code and model weights are publicly available.

item.title: Researchers release ArSciKids, two Arabic datasets for primary school science experiments and multiple-choice questions aligned with curricula in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: ArSciKids is a new collection of two Arabic datasets designed to support curriculum-aligned educational content generation for primary education science. The datasets include 999 manually curated scientific experiment records from official textbooks and 2,167 multiple-choice questions from the Saudi Manhaji platform, covering grades 1-6 with structured annotations such as objectives, procedures, and correct answers. The datasets consist of authentic Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetic data. The researchers fine-tuned ten open language models of varying sizes using LoRA and evaluated their performance with automatic metrics like ROUGE and BLEU, as well as human assessments. Results showed significant differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available to facilitate research in Arabic educational natural language processing, curriculum-aware content generation, and low-resource language modeling.

item.title: Halal-NeSyNet combines DistilBERT and symbolic vectors with clause-scoped cross-attention to improve automated Halal food ingredient auditing and logistics triage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Halal-NeSyNet is a neuro-symbolic model designed to verify Halal compliance in packaged foods by analyzing ingredient declarations and E-number additives with clause-scoped attention. The system addresses cross-clause modifier confounding, where qualifiers in one ingredient clause should not clear unqualified additives in another, using a benchmark of 3,199 items labeled by a 50-code rule base rather than certification authorities. Halal-NeSyNet outperforms text-only TF-IDF baselines, achieving over 97% accuracy and nearly 100% counterfactual triad consistency, with most gains attributed to clause-scoped symbolic features rather than the neural network itself.

item.title: Researchers present MemShift benchmark to separate detection and repair in LLM-derived personal memory, evaluating shifts like source revision and deletion with deterministic scoring [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce MemShift, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI assistants' ability to maintain accurate personal memory by separating the detection of changes from the repair of values derived by language models. MemShift tests five types of shifts-source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export-using synthetic data branches and a deterministic scorer to assess whether the memory notices changes and correctly repairs them. The study evaluates four open-weight language models and finds that detection effectiveness is limited by repair accuracy, with programmatic approaches improving recomputation over LLMs alone. The code and data for MemShift are publicly available.

item.title: Experimental study compares hybrid retrieval, NLI, and open-source LLMs for scientific claim verification, finding Qwen3 8B outperforms others but fusion of models reduces accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted an experimental study to evaluate scientific claim verification using a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact. They compared a DeBERTa-based NLI model against open-source large language models (LLMs) including Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, using a hybrid retrieval method combining semantic and lexical search to provide relevant evidence sentences. Qwen3 achieved the highest Macro-F1 score of 0.7937, outperforming Llama 3.1 and Mistral, while the NLI baseline scored 0.3157.

item.title: Researchers propose VIAS method to improve multi-value alignment in large language models by isolating value-specific activation vectors, enhancing compliance beyond prompting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), a technique that adjusts internal activations of large language models to better align with multiple organizational values simultaneously without changing model weights. VIAS contrasts responses under prompts that include or omit specific values to isolate value-specific activation vectors, reducing overlap and improving multi-value compliance. The method was evaluated on the PROTECT workplace compliance dataset with a 21-value taxonomy, showing that VIAS combined with prompting achieved compliance with all tagged values in 69.6% to 75.2% of scenarios across three different models, outperforming prompting alone. While VIAS reduces vector overlap, it does not fully enable independent control over each value, indicating further work is needed for precise multi-value steering.

item.title: Researchers present SPARK, a multi-episode corrective framework for embodied retrieval-augmented generation that improves knowledge base accuracy through targeted re-observation and selective merging [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SPARK addresses errors in embodied retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems by using a semantic critic to flag knowledge base regions, a planner to generate revisits, and selective merging to update information based on new observations. Evaluated on four outdoor AirSim maps with degraded viewpoints, SPARK improved embodied question answering (EQA) performance while reducing stored objects by 13-41% compared to append-only updates. Multiple corrective episodes further enhanced performance beyond undegraded references. Ablations confirmed the contributions of the critic's signals, targeted revisits, and selective merging to overall gains. This framework demonstrates the importance of correcting embodied memory to reduce accumulated errors as such systems scale.

item.title: Researchers formalize geometric and algebraic inference strategies in humans and neural networks, identifying distinct computational tradeoffs and signatures in transitive reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have formalized two inference strategies-geometric and algebraic-in humans and neural networks, exploring their computational tradeoffs and distinct signatures in transitive inference tasks. The geometric strategy involves shaping representational geometry to reflect relational structure for efficient inference, while the algebraic strategy uses flexible attention to reason over novel relations at a higher computational cost. Experiments demonstrate these strategies in humans, neural networks trained from scratch, and large language models (LLMs). Causal interventions reveal that geometric inference depends on representational geometry and algebraic inference on selective attention mechanisms, paralleling neurobiological disruptions observed in humans. This framework unifies various phenomena in human and machine reasoning and reconciles differing views on cognitive flexibility by showing that both strategies have unique strengths and characterize different aspects of behavior.

item.title: Researchers develop conic programming theory to certify transformer attention robustness, proving NP-hardness of certification and providing tighter bounds than existing methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a conic programming framework to certify the robustness of transformer attention mechanisms against input perturbations, addressing the challenge of bounding output changes in large language models. They identify the bilinear interaction between queries and keys as the core difficulty, proving that certification is NP-hard over input boxes and inapproximable when attention logits vary by a constant amount, while fixed queries allow efficient worst-case computation. The proposed exponential cone moment relaxation achieves quadratic error bounds in perturbation radius and outperforms linear bound propagation methods in tightness. Computational experiments on GPT-2 demonstrate the practical applicability of the theory, confirming its predicted accuracy and tighter certification bounds across attention heads.

item.title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.00606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribution graphs over the features of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to predict what an ablation does and are compared across training seeds. A TopK SAE keeps the largest preactivations at each token, and a feature's margin is its preactivation's distance to the cutoff. On five public TopK SAE pairs from three Pythia models, zeroing one feature moves a next layer feature across the cutoff in 0.74 of cases or more, and the crossings carry most of the response's energy. Over writes that scale a feature's code by three factors, the graph built on the features active beforehand has a median relative error of 0.247 or more. The margin graph adds the first order change to every preactivation and reranks, at the same cost, and errs by at most 0.033. At the median, the crossing features' decoded change is 1.24 times the model's own change in norm or more. Between seeds of one testbed, sparse maps between features explain 0.85 of a graph's energy on its active features, and 0.47 once the other seed's graph keeps only its own. The largest model studied is pythia-160m.

item.title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
item.description: arXiv:2611.01313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking

item.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.01460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

item.title: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.01496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Representation steering methods like difference-in-means (DIM) offer a lightweight approach to controlling LLM behavior, but their effectiveness varies widely across concepts, datasets, and layers, making principled deployment costly without exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps. We build on the discriminability index $d'$, a compute-cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive training activations separate along the steering direction. Across five behaviors on 3 models, we demonstrate uses beyond its established role as a dataset-level steerability predictor. First, in the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting, we show that $d'$ reliably identifies performant layers at which to steer, eliminating the need for a layer-wise sweep. Second, we extend this analysis to open-ended multi-token generation, and find that $d'$ remains successful for layer selection across different settings. Lastly, we test whether the position of a generated token's representation on the DIM line predicts steering success on that individual example. In the MCQA setting, this works for high-$d'$ datasets but is inconsistent across behaviors, models, and training-token choices in open-ended generation. This highlights that methods developed and conclusions drawn in single-token MCQA settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.

item.title: CREDO: Evidence-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Temporal Reasoning Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.01643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires language model agents to retrieve evidence, select relevant facts, and perform multi-step temporal reasoning. However, the trajectory-level outcome signal in GRPO does not explicitly distinguish the quality of intermediate decisions: downstream failures can penalize useful evidence acquisition, while identical rewards in all-failed groups eliminate the relative outcome signal despite differences in intermediate progress. We propose Credit Redistribution with Evidence-Driven Opportunities (CREDO), which uses intermediate evidence to recover local supervision, including in all-failed groups, and determine where outcome supervision acts. CREDO assigns positive stage-level credit through comparisons among rollouts of the same question and uses retained answer overlap as an opportunity proxy to shift part of the outcome-policy weight toward reasoning and answering. The framework preserves terminal rewards and trajectory-level advantages, while redistribution conserves total outcome-policy weight per trajectory. Following the public evaluation protocol of prior work, CREDO raises Overall accuracy from 78.0% to 82.4% and Multiple accuracy from 55.0% to 65.6% on MultiTQ relative to the strongest published baseline in our comparison. On TimelineKGQA, it raises cross-KG accuracy from 30.9% to 36.4% relative to our reproduced baseline via direct transfer to ICEWS Actor under matched training and evaluation settings.

item.title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.01747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.

item.title: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.01864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.

item.title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \$1.17 to \$1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \$0.78 to \$0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

item.title: Test-Time Scaling for Open-Ended Reasoning at Small Model Scale [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A vote over a model's samples can only help when the samples disagree. For open-ended generation the binding question is therefore not how to combine samples but whether a model produces samples worth combining, a question test-time scaling has answered for math but not for free-form text. We study it at small scale with semantic cluster voting, a judge-free aggregator that groups a small instruct model's samples by meaning and returns the largest cluster's representative, with no reward model or self-judging. On a 250-prompt benchmark with three tiers of answer checkability, the same pattern holds across three model families (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B) and two generation seeds: voting raises accuracy on the math control, where samples vary but stay checkable (a gain of +10 to +29 points across the three models), yet adds at most +0.30 judge points on open-ended text. On a larger 200-problem MATH-500 run with the primary model, the math gain is +8.5 points (95% CI [+4.0, +13.0]). Almost every open-ended sample falls into one meaning cluster, so there is little to select over. The collapse is consistent with instruction-tuning rather than model size, and raising decoding temperature does not recover usable diversity, because it costs more quality than it adds (net -0.64 judge points, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.37]).

item.title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

item.title: Hinted Scaling Laws [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most $10^{20}$ FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a $10^{23}$ FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to $10^{22}$ FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

item.title: Variable names provide priors: semantic grounding enables data-efficient numerical prediction by large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, from question answering to code generation. Recent studies have found that LLMs can perform numerical prediction on tabular datasets via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear under what conditions and how LLMs use variable names and in-context examples for numerical prediction. Here we show that semantic grounding, the match between variable names and the values they describe, allows five LLMs without task-specific training to match or outperform seven supervised machine learning (ML) models across 20 datasets from nine scientific domains, particularly when examples are scarce. Reasoning traces indicate that variable names allow LLMs to draw on domain-specific knowledge acquired during pretraining. Using controlled tasks based on physical formulas, we further show that LLMs integrate domain-specific knowledge with in-context examples in a way consistent with Bayesian updating. Specifically, when the relationship between the inputs and the target cannot be inferred from the examples alone, LLMs rely on domain-specific knowledge as the prior. Conversely, as contradicting examples accumulate, LLM predictions shift progressively towards these examples, which act as the likelihood. Our work reveals how LLMs use domain-specific knowledge in numerical prediction and positions them as data-efficient predictors for data-scarce scientific domains.

item.title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02779v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage--execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0-61.3x over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27-3.4x on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method's implementations for 16 of 28 templates.

item.title: SelfImprove-Bench: Evaluating Generalization in Self-Improving Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursively self-improving (RSI) systems are increasingly viewed as a promising means of accelerating progress toward artificial general intelligence. They aim to autonomously improve their capabilities by refining their working pipelines and recursively improving the strategies that guide subsequent refinements, with gains generalizing to unseen scenarios.However, existing evaluations lack reliable metrics to distinguish capability gains from scenario fitting, sustainable and extensible protocols for unseen tasks and difficulties, and fine-grained attribution of improvement to evolution traces. To this end, we propose SelfImprove-Bench,an RSI evaluation framework that organizes tasks into three primary capabilities (i.e., Exploring, Planning, Reasoning) as scenarios for guiding model evolution. We instantiated the tasks on games for controllability and reproducibility, and pairs them with scalable generation and orchestration driven by task templates and difficulty coefficients. Beyond task-level scores, SelfImprove-Bench organizes evaluation into generalization ladder levels G0 to G4 that measure how far gains transfer from training conditions. Experiments reveal that the evolutionary gains of existing RSI methods are inconsistent across generalization levels.

item.title: Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents increasingly act on users' behalf by manipulating external environments through tools, often from high-level instructions that leave critical task- and environment-specific context unstated. To prevent resulting misaligned actions, recent work verifies proposed actions before execution, largely by establishing whether the conditions supporting them hold. We argue that this confirmation-oriented view leaves a fundamental blind spot: a wrong action often passes every check that asks whether it is right. This motivates a different question for verification: rather than asking what evidence supports an action, can the agent find evidence that refutes it? We pursue this direction with BlackSwan, a refutation-oriented, expect-suspect-test procedure that predicts the intended effect of each state-mutating action, formulates specific and empirically testable hypotheses for how it could be wrong, and tests them using existing observations or additional non-mutating actions, executing the action only if none survives testing. On challenging AppWorld tasks, BlackSwan improves success rate over the strongest baseline by 14.9 and 25.2%p with and without the backbone model's thinking mode, respectively. Even without thinking or in-context demonstrations, it outperforms stronger baselines equipped with them. The gains also transfer beyond AppWorld, with BlackSwan improving WebShop performance by 12.7%p. More broadly, our results suggest that language model agents have an underused capacity to recognize and self-correct misaligned actions, which can be systematically elicited through active conjecture and refutation before execution.

item.title: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.02956v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical decompositions of predictive uncertainty, such as the information-theoretic one, are defined for a fixed representation $x$ of the input object. They do not consider that $x$ may be incomplete, nor do they measure how much the missing information can affect the prediction. In Large Language Models, users can clarify an underspecified input without any retraining. The clarified input can describe the user's unobserved intent $z^*$ more accurately and change the predictive uncertainty about the outcome. In this paper, we formalize this setting probabilistically and derive a three-term decomposition of prediction risk into specification, residual aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainties. We show that at the original information level, when only $x$ is available, the aleatoric uncertainty, represented by a Bayes risk, has two components. The first, which we call specification uncertainty, is the expected reduction in this Bayes risk from revealing the intent. The second is the residual aleatoric uncertainty, i.e., the Bayes risk that remains once the intent is known, averaged over its possible values $z$ given $x$. The distinction is important, as specification uncertainty informs the decision to request clarification before making a prediction. We build approximations of these components and connect them to existing uncertainty measures. Our experiments across different domains and modalities show distinct roles for the three components. Specification uncertainty is the most informative for detecting underspecified inputs, while residual aleatoric uncertainty is the most informative for detecting in-distribution prediction errors.

item.title: LLMs Depend on Specialist Tools for Out-of-Distribution Generalization in MS/MS Structural Elucidation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.03308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A frontier language model was recently reported to solve 1D NMR structural elucidation without tools. We ask whether this capability transfers to tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) in the de novo setting, where the model must propose a structure directly from the spectrum without a candidate list or reference library. To separate reasoning from recall, we build a 100-analyte benchmark from MassSpecGym, split by each analyte's textual footprint into in-distribution (well documented in literature) and out-of-distribution (essentially undocumented) arms. We hold the model, harness, and output format fixed and vary only the LLM's access to domain-specific tools. Without tools, a frontier LLM reaches 52% Top-1 accuracy in-distribution but only 2% out-of-distribution. Only access to de novo structure generators improves out-of-distribution accuracy, raising it to as much as 38% Top-1, and the resulting agent outperforms the standalone de novo models both in and out of distribution. These results suggest that LLMs are not effective at de novo MS/MS structural elucidation on their own, and that further gains depend on the specialist tools available to the agent rather than on the LLM itself.

item.title: Characterizing When Language Models Take Harmful Actions to Protect Their Assigned Goals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.03374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent language model (LM) safety failures have largely been studied as disparate phenomena. In agentic misalignment, a model blackmails an executive to avoid being replaced. In alignment faking, it complies with harmful requests during training to keep its values from being modified. We argue that these behaviours share a common decision structure: a model assigned a goal must either take a harmful action to preserve it or refuse and lose it. We formalize this as a goal-harm conflict and present the same conflict under various elicitation protocols that range from compact forced-choice prompts to simulated agentic environments. These protocols span two perspectives on LM decision-making, which we term (i) the logit view, reading preferences from answer-token probabilities, and (ii) the sampling view, classifying open-ended responses with an LM judge. Under the logit view, we show that goal importance and harm severity additively shape how a model resolves these value conflicts. Under the sampling view, we derive two factorizations of the harmful-action probability that safety evaluations commonly report. The first measures how well a preference read from answer tokens carries over into behaviour, such as making a harmful tool call. The second attributes a low harmful-action rate either to refusal or to responses that reach no resolution. We then show how fictional context changes a model's preference under the logit view, and how tool use and partial observability -- two features of agentic evaluations -- change its harmful-action rate under the sampling view. Our work offers a descriptive framework for studying how LMs resolve such value conflicts and for estimating low-probability harmful actions at a finer granularity than the aggregate harm rates commonly reported in safety evaluations.

item.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.03526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.

item.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.03577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.

item.title: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.03622v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.

item.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.03634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

item.title: Automated grounding verification of AI statements about chest radiographs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2604.09537v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A grounding verifier checks a statement about a patient's image against the radiology report and the cited evidence. The state-of-the-art methods for testing these verifiers remove or replace the cited evidence while the patient's report stays unchanged. To our knowledge, no existing method checks both the report and the cited evidence. We present Building Report And Citation Examples (BRACE), an automated framework that builds training examples from public radiology reports and Radiopaedia articles. We compared a lexical baseline and 42 verifiers with 0.1-284B parameters on 5 different public chest radiograph datasets. At a threshold accepting 0.90 of the supported test examples, verifiers trained with BRACE accepted a mean of only 0.239 of AI-written statements contradicted by the report. Verifiers trained without contradicted examples passed the state-of-the-art tests, yet accepted most of these statements (0.830 on average). With citations retrieved from held-out Radiopaedia articles, verifiers trained with BRACE accepted 0.169 of AI-written statements with an agreeing report and an unsupporting citation. By contrast, zero-shot large language models mostly checked the report and not the citation (they accepted 0.830 of these statements). We further assessed the framework manually, with two board-certified radiologists independently labeling a sample of test reports. The framework's labels agreed with each radiologist (k > 0.910) almost as closely as the radiologists agreed with each other (k = 0.952). Moreover, instantiating the framework for food allergens in recipes, we showed that it extends beyond clinical applications. A verifier built the same way accepted 0.493 of the statements contradicted by the recipe, whereas a lexical baseline accepted 0.898. Using both the report and the cited evidence, verifiers trained with BRACE could check AI statements before clinicians read them.

item.title: When Evidence is Sparse: Weakly Supervised Early Failure Alerting in Dialogs and LLM-Agent Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.05414v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Early failure alerting requires deciding, while a dialog or agent trajectory unfolds, whether it is likely to fail. Existing approaches broadly follow two directions. LLM-based uncertainty monitoring either elicits confidence from the acting model, tying reliability to its own self-assessment, or queries an external frontier judge at each prefix, incurring costly repeated inference. Trained monitors instead either rely on per-turn annotations, which are rarely available, or train every prefix to predict the terminal outcome without explicitly modeling where failure-indicating evidence appears. We address these limitations with a lightweight external monitor trained only from trajectory-level outcomes, motivated by a pattern across five benchmarks: turns rated highly relevant to failure are sparse and often late. Its attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) component learns turn-level contributions from trajectory outcomes and distills them into online evidence features that complement prefix predictions. We pair the resulting failure estimates with $\alpha$-STOP, a single preference-conditioned policy that selects accuracy-earliness operating points at inference time. The predictor improves Pareto-frontier quality (hypervolume) by 1-10% over naive prefix supervision, while the full system improves it by 3-42% over state-of-the-art trigger policies without per-preference retraining. By avoiding repeated frontier-model calls, our lightweight monitor reduces measured per-decision serving cost by 1,103-3,749$\times$ and latency by 31-106$\times$ relative to the LLM-based uncertainty monitor (GPT-5.2).

item.title: Reasoning Consensus: Structural Ensembling of LLM Reasoning via Weighted DAG Aggregation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.27783v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) reason in free-form chain-of-thought (CoT) without revealing which steps were well supported and which alternatives were rejected. In high-stakes domains, users then cannot judge if an answer rests on sound reasoning. Majority voting and multi-agent debate improve answers using model agreement, but do not expose agreement on individual steps. Reasoning Consensus (RC) extracts a typed reasoning graph from each CoT, merges equivalent steps across graphs from diverse models, and weights every step by how many chains attest to it. RC reveals this step-wise support and the varied justifications behind each answer. On 7 benchmarks across law, science, medicine, narrative reasoning and logic, RC matches majority voting and debate in accuracy (69.4% vs. 69.0-70.3%). An LLM judge prefers RC's best-supported graph to other graphs for the same answer. In a user study, participants read RC graphs faster than debate transcripts or vote tallies, and 14 of 18 preferred them for future use.

item.title: A Study of ASR Adaptation and Representation Dimensionality Reduction in Persian Speech Emotion Recognition Using Whisper [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.05165v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) in low-resource languages remains a challenging problem due to limited labeled data. In this work, we study the use of Whisper for Persian SER with a particular focus on representation dimensionality reduction and language-specific model adaptation. We propose a SER framework in which frame-level embeddings extracted from the Whisper encoder are reduced in dimensionality using PCA, eliminating the need for learned projection layers and substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. The reduced representations are aggregated using an attention-based pooling mechanism and classified with a lightweight prediction head. In addition, we investigate whether fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task improves downstream SER performance. Experiments conducted on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent evaluation protocol show that PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition performance while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning yields only modest gains for SER, suggesting limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion-related representations under the evaluated conditions. These findings provide practical insights into the efficient use of large pretrained speech models for emotion recognition in low-resource languages.

item.title: Entity-Aware Evaluation of OCR Systems for Historical Document Transcription [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.33004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is essential for digitizing historical archives, yet standard evaluation metrics such as Character Error Rate (CER) do not necessarily reflect whether meaningful information, such as names, dates, and identifiers, is preserved. In this work, we investigate entitylevel analysis of OCR errors as a complementary perspective for evaluating OCR quality in historical documents. Using a publicly available benchmark of 175 documents from the Berrutti Archive, augmented with 5,209 manually annotated entity mentions that will be released upon acceptance, we compare sequence-recognition OCR systems, OCR-specialized vision-language models, and general-purpose vision-language models. Beyond global transcription accuracy, we analyze entity preservation and recoverability under varying character-level edit tolerances. Our experiments show that OCR rankings depend on the evaluation criterion: while Qwen 3.6 achieves the highest entity coverage across all tested tolerances, several systems with lower exact-match coverage recover substantially when small errors are tolerated, suggesting that many of their errors correspond to localized character-level deviations rather than fundamentally incorrect entity transcriptions. Conversely, some systems remain unable to recover many entities even under relaxed matching. These findings show that OCR quality cannot be fully characterized by aggregate transcription metrics alone and highlight the importance of evaluating how OCR errors affect the preservation and recoverability of meaningful information.

item.title: T2D: Target-to-Draft Model Pruning & Adaptation for Efficient Speculative Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.34103v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.

item.title: When Should LLMs Be Less Specific? Selective Abstraction for Reliable Long-Form Text Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2602.11908v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLMs are widely used, yet they remain prone to factual errors that erode trust and limit adoption in high-risk settings. One approach to mitigate this risk is to equip models with uncertainty estimation mechanisms that abstain when confidence is low. However, this binary "all-or-nothing" approach is excessively restrictive in long-form settings, often discarding valuable information. We introduce Selective Abstraction (SA), a framework that enables LLMs to trade specificity for reliability by selectively reducing the detail of uncertain content. We formalize SA through selective risk and coverage, and propose Atom-wise Selective Abstraction, a claim-level instantiation that decomposes responses into atomic claims and replaces uncertain atoms with higher-confidence, less specific abstractions. We develop a novel end-to-end pipeline for evaluating long-form generation that instantiates risk as factual correctness and measures coverage as retained information. Our comprehensive empirical evaluation across five LLMs and two long-form factual benchmarks shows that atom-wise SA consistently improves the risk-coverage trade-off, outperforming seven baselines, including claim removal, self-revision, sampling-based aggregation, and chain-of-verification. It improves AURC by up to 35.61% over claim removal, demonstrating that reducing specificity boosts reliability while preserving substantial information. We further provide a risk-guided procedure for selecting a confidence threshold that satisfies a target risk.

item.title: MoBiQuant: Mixture-of-Bits Quantization for Token-Adaptive Any-Precision LLM [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2602.20191v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic runtime latency and memory constraints necessitate flexible large language model (LLM) deployment, where an LLM can be inferred with various quantization precisions based on available computational resources. Recent work on such any-precision quantization either relies on hardware-inefficient vector quantization or induces additional scaling factors when switching between bit-widths. Meanwhile, existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods calibrated for a fixed low precision show poor generalizability under runtime precision change. In this work, we attribute the source of poor generalization across bit-widths to a precision-dependent outlier migration phenomenon where the distribution of PTQ-sensitive tokens changes across precisions. Motivated by this observation, we propose MoBiQuant, a novel any-precision Mixture-of-Bits quantization framework that adjusts weight precision for flexible LLM inference based on token sensitivity. Specifically, we propose a many-in-one recursive residual quantization that can iteratively reconstruct higher-precision weights at runtime and mitigates outlier migration with a token-aware router to dynamically select the optimal inference precision of each token.Extensive experiments show that MoBiQuant matches or surpasses frontier single-precision PTQ while exhibiting strong elasticity, achieving significant memory savings and throughput gains of up to $1.34\times$ over state-of-the-art any-precision methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/SimWangArizona/MoBiQuant.

item.title: SYN-DIGITS: A Synthetic Control Framework for Calibrated Digital Twin Simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2604.07513v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Persona simulation based on large language models---often referred to as digital twin simulation---is increasingly used for market research, recommender systems, and social science research. However, these simulations often exhibit systematic bias and miscalibration relative to real human behavior. We propose SYN-DIGITS, a model-agnostic, post-hoc calibration framework that learns relationships among questions from digital twins and transfers them to predict human responses. We focus on a cold-start setting in which no human response to the target question is observed, so calibration must rely on digital twins and human data on reference questions. Our analysis shows that, though digital twins may not reproduce individual human responses accurately, they can capture nontrivial relationships among questions that can be effectively transferred to the human side. When individual-level data is unavailable and we only have access to marginal information on reference questions, our framework also supports distribution-level calibration for predicting the distribution of human responses on the target question. Across three datasets and thirteen persona constructions, experiments show that SYN-DIGITS achieves 11% to 417% relative improvements in individual-level correlation and 46%--57% relative reductions in distributional discrepancy compared to uncalibrated baselines.

item.title: Selective Linkage Precision for Released Medical Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.02276v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hospitals may release de-identified chest radiographs while restricting access to their reports. An attacker who already has reports from the same population and their metadata can use a vision-language model (VLM) to match images to reports. We introduce selective linkage precision, which measures correct matches among the highest-confidence queries after filtering candidates by the available attributes. Across 8 public VLMs and 3 chest radiograph datasets, the maximum whole-pool Recall@1 is 0.40%. However, this metric averages over every query without attribute filtering. On ReXGradient-160K, MedSigLIP-448 reaches 67.68% precision at a budget of 100 after filtering by sex, age band, and projection, with a median of 327 candidate reports. On the same eligible query set, an attribute-only policy reaches 24.99% and the model alone reaches 1.98%. Adding acquisition year, available in only 1 of the 3 datasets, yields 99.05% precision and a median of 24 candidates. Uniform guessing on the observed selected queries has an expected precision of 19.91%. Expanding the primary-setting collection to all 123,100 ReXGradient studies lowers precision to 37.23%. On BioViL-T, the tested head finetuning procedures do not lower linkage below the public checkpoint. Selective linkage precision requires inference without retraining and could help hospitals evaluate which attributes to publish.

item.title: TRACER: Token ReAssignment for Concept ERasure in Generative Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.07688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative recommendation formulates next-item prediction as autoregressive generation over semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from users' historical interactions, making modern recommender systems structurally similar to large language models (LLMs). As privacy and safety concerns grow, these systems increasingly require concept unlearning to remove sensitive or harmful concepts associated with items. However, existing LLM unlearning methods cannot be directly applied to generative recommendation. Unlike word tokens with explicit semantics, SIDs are abstract identifiers that are often shared by both forget and retain items, leading to severe conflicts between concept removal and recommendation utility preservation. To address this challenge, we propose TRACER, an end-to-end concept unlearning framework based on token reassignment. Rather than directly suppressing shared SIDs, TRACER reassigns concept-related items to alternative tokens that better facilitate forgetting while minimizing side effects on retained items. We further introduce a coherence regularizer to preserve semantic consistency among retain items during unlearning. Experiments on real-world recommendation datasets demonstrate that TRACER effectively removes target concepts while substantially better preserving recommendation utility than existing unlearning baselines.

item.title: Wrong but Useful: Trajectory Value Beyond Answer Correctness in Multi-Agent Messages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.14375v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A solution can end with a wrong answer and still help another solver. In multi-agent reasoning, evaluating only a message's proposed answer can therefore miss its contribution to the receiver. We measure this contribution as trajectory value: the change in a fixed integrator's probability of answering correctly when a cached message is present rather than removed. Controlled replay across five benchmarks and two model families separates message effects from identical-input variation. The strongest evidence is for Gemma: in a pre-registered fresh-call re-test, 34 of 73 selected wrong-answer messages pass individual confirmation, exceeding control-calibrated upper bounds on expected false confirmations of 11.4--20.8. The finding is benchmark-dependent and the conservative criterion no longer passes without SciBench. A blinded two-author audit supports the selected answer labels, while neutral replacements show that the helpful effect is not explained solely by message length and position. On held-out replay blocks of the same problems, a message-specific removal rule improves accuracy over the strongest tested correctness-only rule by 1.61 percentage points [1.01, 2.25]. Post hoc analysis localizes most of this gap to pools containing no correct proposal. Evidence for gpt-oss is weaker, and the tested predictors do not establish a practical way to identify useful errors in advance. The results support measuring answer correctness and receiver benefit separately, with value understood as conditional on the message pool, receiver and generation format.
